1.	Is the government conducting research into the effects of long term soil pollution with herbicides, pesticides, and other agricultural chemicals and, if so, at which institutions, and under whose direction is such research being conducted?
2.	What is the annual cost to the government of each of these projects?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
1 and 2. The Department of Agriculture has been directing the attention of available scientists to define where long term pollution may become a problem as the result of agricultural uses of pesticides. At the present time no comprehensive co-ordinated program has been developed or put into action due to the shortage of qualified trained staff. Chemists and biologists capable of conducting the investigations are available now at a few locations, working on local and regional problems of priority that have emerged as the result of local requirements for pest control. The Department of Agriculture is attempting to recruit and train the specialists required to develop research programs at key locations.
Investigations now in progress at research branch establishments as part of existing programs are:
Research station, Kentville, Nova Scotia, director, Dr. J. R. Wright. Investigation of the persistence of pesticides in soil of apple orchards and pastures; the translocation of mercury in apples, vegetables and root crops; the residues in plants and soil from new selective systemic insecticides. Estimated annual cost $20,000.
Research station, Fredericton, New Brunswick, director, S. Hilton. Residues of arsenic and D.D.T. on apples resulting from apple maggot and blueberry maggot control. Estimated annual cost $6,000.
Analytical chemistry research service, Ottawa, Ontario, director, R. B. Carson. Research on methods of pesticide residue analysis in plants, animal and soil. Estimated annual cost $35,000.
Entomology laboratory, Chatham, Ontario, officer in charge, G. F. Manson. Research on factors affecting the efficiency and persistence of soil insecticides. Estimated annual cost $27,000.
Research institute, London, Ontario, director, Dr. E. Y. Spencer. Research on chemistry of metabolism and degradation of pesticides; fundamental research on physiology and toxicology of mode of action of pesticides; physiology and chemistry of natural and synthetic

plant growth regulating compounds; the chemistry and biogenesis of naturally occurring plant toxins and protective substances produced by plants. Estimated annual cost $135,000.
Research station, Winnipeg, Manitoba, director, Dr. A. E. Hannah. Research on the persistence of dieldrin in cereals and forage plants, (program now being revised); chemistry of conversion of heptachlor to hepta-chlor epoxide and factors affecting efficiency of this pesticide in soil (under review). Estimated annual cost $35,000.
Research station, Summerland, British Columbia, director, Dr. C. C. Strachan. Chemical analysis of pesticide spray deposits as part of program of development of local pest control recommendations. Estimated annual cost $13,500.
Research station, Vancouver, British Columbia, director, Dr. R. E. Fitzpatrick. Research on persistence in soil of insecticides used for wireworm control. Estimated annual cost $7,000.

maintopic: REDUCTION IN UNIVERSITY NAVAL TRAINING UNITS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: REDUCTION IN UNIVERSITY NAVAL TRAINING UNITS
speechtext:
While I have the floor, Mr. Speaker, I should like to reply to a question raised on Monday last by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) with respect to the closing down of certain Royal Canadian Navy university training units. In reply I told the hon. member that since this related to a general reorganization of all university training units I would give a full explanation later in the week.
As hon. members will recall, during the course of the debate on the estimates of the Department of National Defence in December of last year I stated that it was intended to reduce expenditures on the university reserves training plan by 50 per cent. Since that time detailed studies have been made within the department and, in consultation with the national conference of Canadian universities and colleges, it has been decided that university training will be done on an integrated basis with only one integrated unit at each university where training is conducted. Theoretical training will be based on the syllabus of the Canadian service colleges. Practical training will be given by the individual services. The implementation of this plan, however, is related to the integration of national defence headquarters and the development of the appropriate administrative procedures. In consequence it will not be practical to reorganize units on an integrated basis before September, 1965.
Inquiries of the Ministry
In the meantime, in order to effect the necessary economies to which I referred last December, certain steps have been taken by the three individual services. In so far as the Royal Canadian Navy is concerned, it has been decided to close eight units at the following universities: University of Alberta, University of Western Ontario, l'universite de Sherbrooke, Bishop's University, Ontario Agricultural College, Mount Allison University, St. Francis Xavier, Acadia University and St. Dunstan's University. In so far as the army and air force are concerned, the existing units will be maintained but strengths will be reduced.
In arriving at this decision the individual needs of each service have been considered. The Royal Canadian Navy, because of the reorganization of the Royal Canadian naval reserves, considered that it was not economically feasible to retain training units whose graduates cannot be absorbed into the active list of the parent Royal Canadian naval reserve divisions. With this as a general criterion, all U.N.T.D. units have been assessed on the basis of proximity to associated reserve divisions, enrolment patterns and efficiency. The army, despite the planned reduction in the militia, can absorb the officers from the C.O.T.C. and, because of the dispersion of the militia, geographical considerations are not too important. The R.C.A.F. elected to have smaller intakes and strengths in the university reserve training plan in order to retain their representation and still bring about the necessary economies.
The hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) asked whether representatives were heard from the universities concerned. In reply I can say that from the outset the department consulted the national conference of Canadian universities and colleges requesting their assistance and advice. The national conference of Canadian universities and colleges was provided with information as plans were developed. Representatives of this organization also met with myself and departmental representatives and their advice and opinions, based on information obtained by them from the universities, was welcomed and suggested changes were made to the extent compatible with budget limitations.

The house resumed, from Tuesday, September 15, consideration in committee on the following resolution-Mr. Hays-Mr. Lamou-reux in the chair.
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the extension of credit to farm machinery syndicates for the purchase of farm machinery and for the terms and conditions of such loans, the amount of a loan not to exceed 30 per cent of the actual price to the farm machinery syndicate of the farm machinery to be purchased with the loan; and to provide also for the establishment in the consolidated revenue fund of a special account not to exceed $25,000,000 to which shall be charged advances made to the Farm Credit Corporation and to which shall be credited all moneys paid to the Receiver General by the corporation and for other financial provisions in relation to the said fund in connection with the administration of the measure.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in rising to continue my remarks on this resolution I might say, in summarizing my remarks last evening, that I had a certain fear this measure would bring about further erosion of the principle which we established in connection with farm credit in 1960. This principle has become well established and has been widely accepted and acclaimed by farm unions throughout Canada. The principle of which I speak was enunciated in the legislation, and clearly stated that the legislation was to aid those who needed aid, while those who were already on an economic unit or had sufficient capital could not obtain a loan from the Farm Credit Corporation.
I feel I should express some of the fears I have, before the bill is presented to us. We hear much talk about the reduction in the number of farms. A few years ago there were something like 600,000 farms in Canada but today there are only 480,000. From time to time economists and agricultural professors have said the sooner the small farmer was done away with the better it

would be, but I disagree with that theory. I believe there is ample room in Canadian agriculture for the small and big farmer alike. There is enough diversification to make room for all types of farmers.
Parliament should be concerned with helping those who need help most, in other words the small farmers, who should be assisted to diversify and intensify their operations. Parliament should not be concerned with helping the large farmers commercialize and go into vertical integration. A few years ago this was the fear being expressed in farm papers and magazines. They all carried articles and editorials saying we must do something about vertical integration. On the other hand, there was and still is a great deal of talk in farm journals about maintaining the family farm.
I want the minister to tell us what this legislation will do. Will it speed up vertical integration, or will it sustain and aid the family farm? The policy of all parties has been to assist the family farm, and I ask how does this legislation help it? I fear it will do more good for vertical integration and for those who want to promote vertical integration than it will for the family farm. One of the few things the farmer treasures and is prepared to work for is his independence, but with vertical integration the very root of his independence is taken away.
This resolution speaks about the establishment of farm machinery syndicates. Why not call them farm machinery integrated farms? I strongly suspect that this legislation will do nothing for the family farm but will promote vertical integration.
It may be asked how can I, a farmer, be against putting more money into the hands of farmers. This legislation with one hand will do that, but as a legislator I must examine where, how, and to what farmers this money will be given. It is my duty to ask myself will this promote and aid my neighbours and the farmers in my constituency, or will it aid and promote big business? Will it aid and encourage the part time farmer? I greatly fear it will. Will this legislation aid the lawyers, doctors, dentists and all those types of people who are buying farms and going into the agriculture business? I fear it may. We farmers are proud of one thing, our independence. We make up our own minds where and when to buy and when to sell, but integration takes this away.
Farm Machinery
This measure will assist in the effort to reduce machinery costs. A few years ago we heard much about the cost-price squeeze, and this squeeze is just as evident today as it was then, in fact more so. In the middle 1950's the farmers were caught in a drastic cost-price squeeze, but due to a great deal of work done by this party when it formed the government, between 1958 and 1962, that problem was alleviated to some degree. I have here a newspaper clipping dealing with the farmers' cost index, showing that their costs rose to a high of 282 points in April last. Two or three years ago the index stood at about 242 points; thus it has risen some 40 points in the last few years.
A publication issued by the dominion bureau of statistics in July, dealing with the index of farm prices, showed that the price index for all Canada was down to 252 points. A year ago it was 271, and two years ago it was 281. In this situation the farmers again face the severe crisis they were in a few years ago, and I ask what will this legislation do to alleviate that problem.
When the Minister of Agriculture spoke in Lethbridge on April 11 last he talked about parliament and how the opposition was filibustering at that time. According to the government, filibustering is all the opposition does. Whenever anybody on the opposition benches makes a speech, according to the government he is filibustering; but today, so that I may set the record straight, I am expressing my fears with regard to this proposed legislation.
At Lethbridge the minister dealt with many matters, and subsequently the Lethbridge Herald carried an editorial entitled "The Farmers Wait". The minister dealt with the three important measures he intended to place before parliament, and the editorial said:
Most important of the three, according to Mr. Hays, is a measure to deal with the high cost of capitalizing a modern-day farming operation. The machinery necessary for good farming is so expensive that it seriously affects the degree of good farming. Exactly what he proposes to do about it Mr. Hays does not say, because the government is expected to save its policy announcements for the House of Commons. But he does promise that his bill would vastly change the agricultural economy.
How will this measure change the agricultural economy? According to the minister it will change it vastly, but I ask in what direction? Is it going to promote vertical integration? Is this the way the minister is going to change it? I suggest this measure will speed up vertical integration and I see nothing in

Farm Machinery
mark-up is 25 per cent. You take off the 20 per cent, and it still leaves you with 5 per cent clear profit for handling the paper work". The syndicate puts up no money at all as a down payment. This is one way in which you can get around this proposed legislation.
There are many questions I would like to ask in this connection. One is, what is "machinery"? What does the minister mean by "farm machinery"? There are a number of farm implements that I think should be classified as farm machinery and on which Canadian farmers are still paying duty. Last evening I mentioned the cattle feeding industry. The hog feeding industry is another example. It is certainly becoming highly mechanized, and is a prominent industry in the agricultural field in Canada. Most of the self-feeding equipment that is brought into Canada from the United States carries a duty of 22J per cent. Is the minister seriously considering bringing down the cost of machinery? If he is, why does he not take off this 22| per cent duty which applies to much of the self-feeding equipment that is now being used in the feeding industry generally in agriculture?
I take the dairy industry, for example. This is a big industry in Ontario and in Quebec. There is duty on much of the dairy equipment, even down to stainless steel milk pails and stainless steel cans. The duty on both these items is 20 per cent. What is the purpose of this duty? Is the minister seriously trying to bring about a reduction in the cost of farm machinery, or is he trying to enhance the image of the minister himself across the country by bringing in this syndicate legislation?

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I have just a few brief remarks to make, and I will take the risk of being embarrassed by the minister when he brings in the bill. I was wondering about certain types of machinery and whether they would qualify for syndicate buying, if I may use that term. I have in mind something that could be of benefit to a number of farmers in the foothills country, for example. I refer to brush clearing equipment. With regard to my own area, perhaps large grass seeding equipment could be purchased; perhaps large portable grain mills. I wonder whether portable grain dryers would be included. This equipment would have been put to great use if the wet weather had continued on the prairies. Also, would portable grain cleaning equipment and seed cleaning equipment be in-

eluded? In other words, would a farmer and his neighbours be permitted to buy this type of equipment under this legislation?
I would like to ask the minister this question. Could a group of farmers set up a cattle feeding co-operative and borrow something like $75,000, as was suggested by the hon. member for Medicine Hat, for equipping a cattle feeding operation, a hog feeding operation, a turkey feeding operation, or an operation of a similar type? Could a syndicate buy this type of machinery duty free, if any duty applied to it? Much of the duty that does apply to machines used on farms involves machines that have a dual purpose, which are agricultural in some aspects and commercial in others.
As I understand the interpretation of this proposed legislation, it is intended to promote commercial ventures, custom work, and so on. If a person was going into the grain drying business, could he buy the grain dryer duty free, for example; or could he buy seed cleaning equipment, grain mills, brush clearing equipment and grass seeding equipment duty free? If duty does apply to this machinery, could it be bought duty free? If it could, approximately 22 per cent would be saved in regard to most of this machinery. This is certainly well worth considering, because 22 per cent of the cost of the high priced machinery used in today's agricultural economy represents a great deal of money.
I have another question that I would ask the minister. In my part of the country during the past year we experienced a great water shortage. P.F.R.A. did a tremendous job in pumping water to the livestock of many farmers. Could farmers' co-ops be set up through which farmers would be able to purchase their own pipe? This would be of some benefit in the drier parts of Alberta. In many areas throughout the southern part of Alberta farmers have gone into the business of hauling water and have bought trucks for this purpose to haul water for their livestock. Could such equipment be bought on a syndicated or cooperative basis? One would wonder whether many other pieces of equipment-I am sure many hon. members have a number of pieces of equipment in their minds-will qualify under this legislation.
I should also like to see the minister take an active interest in the price of farmers' commodities. Some time ago the turkey producers were alarmed at the removal of quotas on turkeys from the United States coming into Canada. It seems to me that the minister
Farm Machinery
shrugged this off rather lightly, and said in effect; "Everything is all right in the industry. You fellows will have to take a few cents less but don't worry about it. You can eat your own turkeys, I guess, if you get really hungry". That was the sort of attitude he had.
The lamb industry, which at times is a flourishing one in southern Alberta, has suffered a severe drop in price of eight cents a pound over the last six months. Has the minister paid attention to this problem and what is he prepared to do about it?
With regard to the beef industry, I mentioned some time ago that the minister pointed out last year that this was one part of the agricultural economy where optimism was evident. However this has certainly not shown to be the case this year, in fact even in the fall of 1963. Prices and optimism in the beef industry are at an all time low, at least since the last ten years. I have never seen the industry look at its future so dismally. Some months ago I asked the Minister of Agriculture what he proposed to do about the red meat embargo placed on Canadian red meat entering the United States. I asked him twice as a matter of fact, but he never got around to giving me an answer. Perhaps the minister could make a more direct and interested appraisal of the price aspect of the agricultural economy so that the farmers can buy and pay for machinery to enable them to become more efficient.
There are just two or three recommendations which I should like to place on record regarding the manufacturing industry, particularly that part of it engaged in farm machinery manufacture. During the study of this question by the agriculture committee in 1961 I had some points brought home to me with regard to dealers being able to return spare parts which they no longer required. Actually companies do allow for return of parts. They have what they call a parts returnable list; but if a particular part is no longer saleable you can rest assured, Mr. Chairman, that it is not on the returnable list. Therefore this increases the overhead and the dealers' costs. Dealers should be able to return all parts to the manufacturer, and the amount of money paid for them should be refunded. That would lower the cost of handling spare parts and eventually lower the cost to the farmer. Dealers should also be able to stock the cheapest part for any particular machine whether or not the part be made by the company with which he has a dealership. I think it was pointed out time and again in the agricultural committee that

Farm Machinery
every company had a different price for the same sort of bearing. A dealer should be able to stock or buy from the manufacturer the same bearing at the cheapest price.
There must also be more standardization. Time and again in the agricultural committee evidence was submitted that not enough was done by the machine companies to standardize their equipment. In fact it is obvious to many farmers that machine companies go out of their way to make their parts just a little different from the parts of other manufacturers so that other parts cannot be used on their machines. Companies such as Hydraulic Couplers, and many more companies who manufacture repair parts, could in this way bring about a greater reduction in cost of spare parts and repairs to machinery to the benefit of the farmers.
I think the whole matter of dealership contracts should be examined by the combines investigation branch or the whole question referred, as I suggested last evening, to the agricultural committee. The whole distribution system of agricultural machinery should be given close examination. Actually in the 1960-61 inquiry the committee dealt more with the cost of production than with the distribution system. Canadian Co-operative Implements Limited, for example, which had brought in and innovated a new distributing system, was not even heard from during the committee inquiry, and I think this whole question should be dealt with once again. This method of syndicated buying which the government is now promoting could be examined by the agricultural committee to see whether or not it would promote vertical integration or the family farm. It appears obvious to me-I do not want to be embarrassed but, as I said, I run the risk of being embarrassed-that in promoting this resolution the government is sponsoring the virtual take-over of farming in Canada. It has discarded and done away with the principle every political party has stood for hitherto, namely the promotion and maintenance of the family farm. It is just one more manifestation of the millionaire's approach to the agricultural problems in Canada today.

I really had not intended to take part in this discussion of the resolution before the committee, until I heard the minister inform us that there was no point in anybody speaking on the resolution because all the answers were contained in the bill. That in itself would make me, as one who believes in democracy and parliamentary procedure and who has some respect for those

institutions, rise from my seat and loudly complain that the minister already knows what is in the bill, that this resolution is only window dressing, and that although he will get some very good ideas from members of parliament he will give no consideration to them. This in effect is direction of legislation at its worst, because I presume that this bill in particular will follow, not the wishes of the cabinet or the farm organizations, but rather the inclination of the minister himself. Therefore I strongly protest, Mr. Chairman, at the minister's admitting publicly that he has no use for our parliamentary traditions, which ask the government to present a resolution when any legislation involving major expenditure is required. He may not agree that these resolutions serve any purpose, and I realize that the Liberal government are seeing less and less use in them, but I think it is shocking when a minister gets up and says, in effect: "Get on with the bill; I already have the particulars in it, this is only window dressing".

Well, Mr. Chairman, I accept the minister's explanation, which is not what I interpreted from his original remarks. However, as I say, I accept what the minister says in its inclination. This was not clear to me from the previous explanation. I think that the minister, every farm organization in Canada and every member of parliament who has given any consideration to the farm problem at all will know that one of the major problems that Canada's farmers face is the increase in the cost of the machinery they require to conduct their agricultural operations. I think this fact is reconized by everyone. I believe anyone who really gives consideration to the problem of the high cost of farm machinery, which has been accompanied by the extending of acreages in order to provide economic family farms, will come to the conclusion that the problem is not that the farmer needs to borrow money

to buy new machinery but rather it is the cost of that farm machinery in relation percentagewise to the operation of the enterprise that the farmer may have.
If the minister gives any consideration to the reports of the farm implement companies I think he will come to the conclusion that there is a great deal to be desired in the operations of the farm machinery companies in Canada. In fact some consideration must be given to the whole international farm machinery industry, because if any industry is international it is this one. It might be interesting for members of the committee to review the proceedings of the agricultural committee several years ago when this matter was being considered. They will find that some farm implements sold in Timiskaming are produced in India and that farm machinery sold in other parts of Canada is made in the United States, Great Britain, France, in fact most of the major countries of Europe as well as in some of the countries of Africa and South America. Many of these machinery companies decide that a particular machine will be manufactured in one country, and its manufacture will not be duplicated anywhere else in their vast international empires.
Knowing the minister's background, knowing something about conditions in western Canada and having heard over the years about the co-operatives that have been established in western Canada both to operate farms and for the pooling of machinery, I think this legislation will work to a limited extent. I also suggest that it will work not only in the case of very large producers but in some instances in the case of very small producers who may be unable to get custom work done by an entrepreneur because their farms are too poor and their acreage too small to warrant the custom operator buying equipment in a particular area.
I make the prediction that the legislation we are now being asked to pass, with regard to which the farm magazines throughout Canada will give great credit to the minister for having tried to solve the problem, will never apply to even 2 per cent of the agricultural population of this nation. If this is true, then this legislation certainly is not the answer to the agricultural problem created by the high cost per unit of farm machinery. If this is true, then the minister had better look far beyond this legislation because I think the problem is much deeper.
The committee that dealt with this matter several years ago came to a number of conclusions. Members can look them up for
Farm Machinery
themselves. I will not bore the committee by reading them. But members should look at them because I believe these conclusions caused the Conservative government of the day a great deal of concern. They raised problems that the Minister of Finance in the present government has tried to solve as did the minister of finance in the former government, and in both cases they have been wholly unsuccessful.
I refer to the fact that American companies, in fact, even some with their headquarters in Canada, are operating international cartels in the farm machinery implement industry, and the government, the Minister of Finance and nobody else in this country has been able to come to grips with this problem. Suggestions were made at the time of the committee hearings that there would have to be controls. We have some controls. There are controls on the import and export of many commodities. But have we had the initiative to place import and export controls on farm machinery? No; this is a totally neglected field. The hon. member for Acadia referred to hydraulic couplers for tractors, ejector seats and other accessories for farm equipment which are subject to taxes and tariff restrictions if bought separately. Milking machinery is also subject to restrictions. But in the main, farm machinery can flow across international borders without any control. This means that the companies pay no attention to supply and demand, produce in areas where it is most economical for them to do so and sell in a market where they can and do command the highest prices which the market will bear.
I am not in a position to say that there are monopolies on the national scene, but when you buy an automobile in Canada, whether from General Motors, Ford, Chrysler or Stude-baker, you find that in comparable categories you get about the same kind of product from one company as you do from another for the same price. I do not know whether or not there is a monopoly. There are many more qualified to judge than I am, but it is a surprising situation and it limits the choice of the individual and his opportunity to get a better deal from one company than from another.
There is a similarity between the farm implement industry and the automobile industry. A John Deere tractor costs very nearly the same as a Massey-Harris tractor of similar horsepower, and with similar equipment. These are problems that the government is not prepared to face. I suggest that the

Farm Machinery
reason the committee was not reconstituted a year ago was that the former government did not have the courage to face these problems. If the minister wants to be fair, if the farm machinery dealers wish to be fair, if the farm magazines wish to be fair, they will point out that this major problem is not being faced by this legislation and has not been faced by this or the former government. In fact, I do not expect it to be faced by any government in Canada for some time, because it will require very drastic controls that the capitalistic governments of Canada are not prepared to impose.
This is the minister's own legislation. In my opinion it does not have the approval of his departmental officials and probably does not have the approval of most of the agricultural representatives in the Liberal party. In saying this I do not wish to be unfair. I represent the farmers of Timiskaming in the main, although incidentally I may represent farmers in other parts of Canada. I represent the mixed farmers of the clay belt of northern Ontario who have problems that are peculiar to them, and my representation is oriented to them. I know that the minister has connections with agriculture in western Canada and I am aware of what type of connections he has. I am sure his representation of his people will be the type of representation that will result in legislation of this kind. This may be all right, except for the fact that this is the Minister of Agriculture presenting this legislation and he' has a much wider responsibility. Under that responsibility he must in my opinion take into consideration the aspirations of farmers in other parts of the country.
Last night I heard a member make the very strong statement that in his opinion most farmers could not get along with their neighbours to the extent of buying farm machinery co-operatively. I believe he was correct. I am in a partnership with my brother, and with two brothers it is very hard to decide whether we are going to cut my fall wheat first or cut his fall wheat first. I will decide that mine is riper and therefore it is necessary to cut it, while I am sure my brother will say that his is the riper and the advantageous time to cut it is today.
Now, Mr. Chairman, in western Canada you can sit around and talk about this for several days before you decide whose wheat you are going to cut. In Timiskaming if you do not get it cut while the sun is shining it will probably rain the next day and you will be lucky if the rain does not last for three weeks.

If it does, no one will get the grain cut. If you do not think this will raise the blood pressure of those operating the farm machinery syndicate, I will be surprised. I suppose a scheme like this will work with people like the Hutterites. It will work with the larger groups in western Canada who have an affinity for one another greater than blood. It will work with those groups who have this type of brotherly philosophy that will allow it to work.
If you have ever dealt with a custom combine outfit or, in the early days, with a threshing outfit you will know that money changed hands in order that one farmer could get his grain cut earlier than his neighbours. There was a little bonus slipped under the table or some kind of incentive used. I presume that sometimes the custom thresher paid some attention to whether or not the cooking at one place was better than another. I know farmers well enough, Mr. Chairman, to know that it would not take very many years before there was a falling out of the members of a cooperative if the weather turned bad and only one or two of the farmers were able to have this equipment at the opportune time, while the others were left out.
The minister, of course, comes from an area in which there is a very dry, very stabilized climate, so probably he does not know about this. However, the situation I have described applies in Ontario and Quebec. I believe the result will be that few farmers will get this type of farm machinery. I imagine the hon. member for Kootenay East may find that a syndicate in his area will be able to go into the pulp and paper industry or a saw mill, something of that nature, because he gets along very well with them. There are a few farmers in my area in the pulpwood industry and they may get along to the extent of being able to share a truck for the hauling of their product. I think that in eastern Canada at least we are going to have some resentment on the part of farmers who find themselves out of luck in getting machinery from the syndicate.
When the minister speaks, as I presume he will, I should like to hear from him what he believes the relationship will be between this legislation and vertical integration. We know that vertical integration, in the fields in which it was introduced originally, has not been successful. It has not been the concern of this government but it was of the previous government because after a period of several years vertical integration in agriculture ran its course. I would suggest that this is an-

other type of vertical integration to which the minister ought to give consideration. I hope he will be interested in doing something in this regard.
Now, Mr. Chairman, supplying credit to purchase farm machinery without cutting the cost of that machinery seems to me to be putting the cart before the horse. All hon. members agree that the price of farm machinery is too high. Farmers do not say they cannot borrow enough money to buy this equipment; they say the price is so high that it is unprofitable to operate it on the farm. We are not cutting the price of farm machinery; all we are doing is supplying credit through the Farm Credit Corporation to enable farmers to group together to buy this machinery. This scheme may or may not cut the cost per farm unit; it may or may not cut the cost of production per unit, but it will not cut the cost of purchasing machinery.
The minister has not told us if this credit is going to cost the farmer 5 per cent. This question, of course, will be answered when we see the bill. We do not know whether or not the banks are going to lend the money and the loan is going to be guaranteed by the government. This is the manner in which farm improvement loans are made. These questions will be answered of course when the bill is introduced. We have met the problem of the reclassification of farm machinery, and I hope the minister has made provision for this in the bill. I am always surprised when I find certain items that are normally included in the cost of a tractor, such things as the canopy, foam rubber seats, a starter and other amenities that we expect on this type of equipment, are not included. When these things are bought separately and not as part of the original unit there is a tariff on them, and this increases the price because those items are not then considered to be farm machinery. This applies to many other things that are normally considered to be part of the tractor or other farm machines. I hope the minister has reclassified the words "farm machinery" so that they include all the things the farmer uses for agricultural purposes. I would presume, Mr. Chairman, that this applies also to trucks used solely for agricultural purposes.
The minister in my opinion has not been fair to farmers or farm organizations, because of his reluctance to say anything about the problem of farm machinery. By now the minister must have read the report of the agriculture committee which conducted a hearing into farm machinery costs. If he has
Farm Machinery
read it, he will note that there are many things the committee studied to which consideration should be given right away. I feel the minister should be prepared to say whether or not he intends to reconstitute this farm machinery inquiry. He ought to be prepared to attempt to arrive at standardization of hydraulic lifts, power take-offs, and things of that sort that are very elementary. The standardization of this type of thing should be easily legislated by the federal government. Does the minister have anything to say about the maintenance of parts at a reasonable cost for a reasonable period of time? The committee thought this was an important part of the farm machinery and implement industry. Has the minister given any consideration to the remarks made last night by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam in relation to the testing of farm equipment? The hon. member pointed out that the provincial governments, particularly Saskatchewan, have gone as far as they can in this field. There is certainly nothing this government is doing better than giving advice and assistance to the provinces to run their own business. This is a field where that could be considered, although I suggest we should do it ourselves rather than have someone else do it.
Has the minister given any consideration to the greatest bugbear in the farm implement industry, namely the problem existing in the used implement end of it? What happens when a farmer trades in an implement? Who gets it and what relation has it to the new implements bought? The minister has said all these questions will be answered when we see the bill. I am quite anxious to see it but I doubt very much that it will answer a lot of these questions, although I hope it answers the questions that have been specifically related to the resolution.
The problems in the farm implement industry and those surrounding methods of reducing the cost per unit of production will have to be answered in many other ways, not all of them in the credit field. The minister will also have to take into consideration the problems he wants the agriculture committee to study. He will have less trouble with farm organizations, the farm press, and indeed with the farmers themselves, if he allows this measure, along with all the others, to be sent to the agriculture committee where they can be discussed, where people who have a great deal of experience and knowledge outside the legislative field would help us to make up our minds on how to supply the

Farm Machinery
fanners with more favourable and satisfactory legislation at less cost to the public and the treasury.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, any legislation introduced in the house to help the agricultural class must necessarily receive the attention of all hon. members, and everyone must see to it that this legislation is enacted as soon as possible.
Yet, it does not mean that we should shelve our responsibilities and take the minister's recommendations for granted.
A few moments ago, when he reiterated his request to the effect that the resolution be passed immediately, my first reaction was to agree. But when I remembered the various questions I asked him, and which remained without answer for many weeks, I revised my way of thinking and agreed with other hon. members that the matter should receive further consideration.
The minister certainly meant well when he introduced this legislation. But, Mr. Chairman, we all know the saying: The road to hell is paved with good intentions. Therefore, in order to warn the minister and help him not commit errors which he would regret later on, I decided to take a few brief minutes to express my views, which are those of my voters at home.
I am very much afraid that the legislation now before us may cause some disappointment, especially among the farmers in the province of Quebec and eastern Canada.
I agree with other hon. members who stated that this measure would affect only an insignificant number of farmers. Moreover, I think what we have here is one more measure tending mainly to help the large farm operators. It seems to me that those are the only measures taken by the present government: measures giving no heed whatever to the family farm or the small farmer.
If there is an important sector in the agricultural field, Mr. Chairman, it is that of the family farm. That is where future farmers learn to work and to till the soil in order to replace their parents. If they are not given the necessary attention, we will sooner or later be the first to suffer the consequences of that carelessness towards that part of our population.
I would like to ask the minister a few questions concerning the measure under consideration. First of all, I would have liked, as other hon. members, to know what he means by farm machinery syndicate. I would have liked to know from the minister whether

these syndicates will be controlled by provincial or federal legislation.
I would have liked also to know what arrangements have been made with the provincial ministers of agriculture during the meetings where this measure has been especially considered.
The minister would certainly have received more attention from this side of the house if, during his remarks, he had explained these points which, I feel, are of vital interest.
We should also like to know the interest rate the borrowers will have to pay; what will be the repayment periods; the amount a syndicate will be able to borrow; and finally whether this legislation will only apply to bona fide farmers or also to citizens who are not farmers.
I am inclined to agree more particularly with my hon. friend from Rosthern (Mr. Nas-serden) when he says that this measure will benefit especially the western farmers and that it ignores the eastern farmers, more particularly those from the province of Quebec, the maritime provinces and Ontario.
I think our people will appreciate the remarks of my hon. friend from Rosthern who is certainly familiar with the needs of eastern farmers.
The question of the price of farm machinery is of capital importance to our farmers. As was pointed out by other speakers, especially the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Horner), the agriculture and colonization committee considered the matter in the spring of 1961. At the time, to get firsthand information, I sent to 200 farmers of my riding a questionnaire in which I asked them to give me some information on the price and life of the farm machinery required to run a family farm. I also told them I needed all the information available to present their case adequately when the question would be considered by the committee.
Out of these 200 questionnaires, I received exactly 72 completed ones. In my first question, I asked this:
Please, indicate, in order of importance, the farm machinery that you think is most important, as well as its purchase price.
In the second question, I asked:
In your opinion, what is the average Hie of the machinery listed under item no. 1.
And my third question read as follows:
Please, list what seems to you the most important reason which explains the increase in price of farm machinery.

Here is what I learned from the answers to these questions sent to professional farmers:
Tractor, $2,300; baling-press, $2,300; manure spreader, $550; mower, $390; spinner, $410; plough, $230; milking machine, $450; harrow, $395; combine, about $4,000; disks, $600; binder, $550; spreader, $400.
Total cost of purchase would be about $12,500, at 1961 prices. The purchasing price of the above farm machinery has certainly increased considerably since then.
Modern farms are also equipped with a hay conditioner, a potato digger, a beet digger and an ensilage cutter or blower. Unfortunately, I have no detail about the price of this machinery, but I am convinced that it is among the most costly.
According to the information obtained by means of that questionnaire, those machines last between five and ten years, depending on the care they receive. Some farmers who are very careful will keep their machinery much longer, while others who are careless will have to make repairs or trade them in much more often than those who keep them in order.
As for the various causes stated to justify the increased cost of machinery, this is what farmers had to say:
First, many are of the opinion that the commissions drawn by salesmen are too high and the profits of the farm machinery manufacturers are exorbitant.
Moreover, repair and maintenance costs are also very high. The same is true for transportation costs which increase constantly from year to year.
They mention also that tax increases that follow one another contribute enormously to the fact that farm machinery gets more expensive every year.
And there are those who even complain that farm machinery, and more particularly tractors, are unnecessarily luxurious.
In this connection, and more especially with regard to tractors, there is surely a great deal of truth in what some farmers told me, because various manufacturers of farm machinery seem to outdo each other in luxury in order to offer de luxe machinery to their customers, even though the latter do not need them to carry out their work. I am sure most farmers could do without de luxe attachments on their tractors. If the cost of those machines were reduced by as much, farmers could use that money for other purposes.
Farm Machinery
According to the replies received, I was able to realize that the farmers, in general, complain about the discrepancy between the cost and the selling price of their products. And this question of farm machinery certainly enters into account when both the prices I have mentioned are being determined.
Then, before resuming my seat, I wish I could, on the part of the farmers of my constituency, exert some pressure upon the minister to have him bring about measures that will particularly apply to the eastern farmers. We are not jealous of the help given to the farmers of the prairie provinces, but we believe that the central government, especially the present Liberal government, following the many promises made, should give special attention to eastern farmers. An eastern department of agriculture was promised, but such a project remains unfulfilled. Consequently, I would ask the hon. minister and his parliamentary secretary, whose intentions are certainly good, to give-

-to have that "long look" of which the minister speaks so often. We need it in eastern Canada today. We need the help of the minister and we do need that "long look". But, even more important, we need practical measures to help our farmers.
Our farmers are most disappointed. I must tell the hon. gentleman this, because it is true. I would much prefer to be agreeable to him and congratulate him on the measures he has brought in. But my farmers-and I am sorry for this-have asked me to tell the hon. gentleman that they are very disappointed. I do not wish to review the measures he has taken-measures which have had results so unfavourable to our dairy farmers. I have told the government this, time and again, but it has not seemed to sink in too well. However, Mr. Chairman, I would like to take this opportunity of saying that there are many facets to this question; there are many angles. We on this side of the house represent so many people who are professional farmers and therefore know very well about farming and farming problems. These people could give the minister a great deal of assistance in arriving at solutions to some of the problems that are today facing our farmers.
I join those who have spoken before me in recommending that this measure be sent to the committee on agriculture and colonization. There is a wealth of knowledge in that committee, especially in members from this

Farm Machinery
side of the house, and we are all willing to help the government because we realize that the Department of Agriculture is in dire need of help. We are willing to give this help to the minister.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a few general remarks at the resolution stage of this legislation. At the outset I would like to quote from yesterday's Hansard, when the Minister of Justice, the house leader, said:
But I think for the benefit of the farmers it would be preferable if we could dispose of the farm machinery syndicates resolution right away.
This may be so, and this is one reason for my rising to my feet, because I am interested in knowing what types of equipment the minister is thinking about in this connection; that is, what types of equipment may be purchased under this legislation. As I see it, farming is pretty well completed for this year, but many farmers wish to lay their plans and arrange their business for the coming year. The word "syndicate" intrigued me, so I looked it up in the Winston dictionary. It says, "Syndicate is an association of persons or corporations to promote some particular enterprise, especially an enterprise requiring a large amount of capital, and control the market in a particular commodity".
This raises the question in my mind as to whether this is a bill mainly for the small farmer who cannot afford a certain type of equipment, or is it going to put some farmers into the category of being more or less small contractors, in terms of equipment costing $50,000 or $75,000? I cannot foresee this bill dealing with some types of farming equipment that we use. I am thinking of haying equipment, loaders, and possibly bulldozers. If one wishes to do bulldozing work, this would be the type of equipment contractors would use for clearing land. Perhaps this is what the minister has in mind, but he has not mentioned it yet. A few minutes ago the minister said that most of the answers were contained in the bill. However, Mr. Chairman, if I understand the position correctly, the resolution stage is the time to put forward ideas that may be introduced into a bill. Despite this, the minister has said the questions have already been answered in the bill.
I would like to point out a few of the difficulties that I think could occur under an arrangement where three or four farmers join together to form a syndicate. I have had some experience, as have many farmers, of buying equipment jointly. I realize that one 
of the drawbacks to this type of co-operative farming is the fact that the farmers will use the equipment and nobody will be its actual boss. Therefore the equipment will not be looked after in the proper manner, and eventually these syndicates about which we are speaking will fall apart. Perhaps again the minister will explain this matter when we deal with the bill. On the other hand, Mr. Chairman, I would think that with regard to any type of equipment costing up to possibly $75,000, the people involved would be organizing for a profit. My idea of a bill that would be of benefit to the small farmers would be one that provided for the purchase of the type of equipment that one would buy in order to save money, and not in order to make a profit.
I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam last evening when he referred to C.C.I.L., as we know it in western Canada, and how it was organized with the idea of saving a great deal of money for the farmers. I believe it is true that many farmers who buy through C.C.I.L. do receive a fair dividend. Again, Mr. Chairman, one of the drawbacks of this arrangement is that only one type of equipment is available and there is no choice. Any farmer who has a specific choice or preference for one particular make of equipment, because he believes it is superior to others, does not fall into this category.
A great deal of the large equipment that C.C.I.L. sells is imported from England, from Europe, and we must realize that when a farmer wants his equipment repaired, he wants the repair to be carried out at once. Anybody who has farmed in western Canada realizes that many times we must have parts flown in from eastern Canada or the United States. I think this is one of the drawbacks of the C.C.I.L. arrangement. Collective parts depots was a subject that was also mentioned. I for one do not believe that this is a feasible set-up. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam mentioned this matter. I do not think there can be co-operation among machine companies any more than there can be between members of different political parties, or members of the House of Commons. I do not think they can agree on one thing.

I believe that a bill such as this, which is of vital interest to farmers all across Canada, should be sent to the committee on agriculture and colonization,

as has been suggested. The committee could then study the bill, and I believe many good suggestions would be brought forward. I hope that when the minister introduces the bill he will specify the types of equipment this legislation will cover. We are looking at the over-all cost of farm equipment, whether it be equipment used in eastern Canada or the large type of equipment used in western Canada. I cannot see that this will have any bearing on lowering the cost of farm equipment. At best it may aid a few of the smaller farmers by enabling them to buy collectively certain types of equipment. The hon. member for Medicine Hat mentioned the figure of $75,000 last evening and I think the minister should tell us whether such a figure is involved here. What types of equipment has he in mind which could possibly cost $75,000. I realize that farm improvement loans have been increased from $7,500 to $15,000, which is all to the good because the cost of equipment has gone up three or four times what it was 15 years ago.
A few other questions I have in mind are these. When we are speaking of partners in a syndicate I should like the minister to explain whether he means such partners will be live partners, or whether just one or two will control the syndicate and the rest will be silent partners. This might again raise the question whether this measure will be of benefit to the small farmer, or will have the effect of organizing a group of big farmers and put them into the farm contracting business.
As we all know, there are many types of tractors and combines today. I would say that the smallest costs about $5,000 to $6,000 and you can pay as much as $12,000 to $15,000. I should like to know whether it is the intention of the minister to allow three or four farmers collectively, after having spent their $15,000 farm improvement loan, to raise another $75,000 to buy some of the bigger tractors and go into commercial custom combining or contract farming.
I should also like to know whether it is the minister's intention that the syndicates be big enough to buy direct from the manufacturer and thus cut out some 40 to 50 per cent profit which is involved in the sale of equipment locally. I am referring to the local dealer who gets about 20 to 25 per cent on selling an implement, and also the wholesalers or general offices located in each province which make, according to the figure I have heard, 35 to 40 per cent for their particular company. That is the profit which eventually ends up

in the hands of the company which manufactures the equipment concerned.
I have just outlined, Mr. Chairman, a few of the questions which I have in my mind. I will not say anything more at this point because I should like to see what is in the bill in detail. When I have seen it I may have either some criticisms or some constructive criticisms, whichever it may be, of the bill which the minister is introducing.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to make a long speech but I do have a few questions to ask the minister at this point. I do not expect him to answer them now, but he might make a note of them and perhaps answer them either on second reading or during committee stage of the bill.
My first question is: Have the officials of his department given consideration to the adequacy of this amount of $25 million? I ask that question because just the other day I was in the Northwest Territories attending a ceremony at which the minister himself was supposed to be present but unfortunately was not. However, his colleague the minister of northern affairs was present and made a speech in connection with the crossing of the Great Slave lake railway into the Northwest Territories, and he referred to the fact that this railroad, among other things would provide a means of transportation across some eight to ten million acres of agricultural land which in due course would be opened up. That is borne out by the fact that in the last four years at least 3,500 to 4,000 applications have been made by people concerned in securing agricultural land in the newly opening areas in the constituency of Peace River alone, under the provincial homestead settlements scheme. The amount of machinery which these farmers and potential farmers would require to remove the brush and cultivate the land will take up a substantial portion of the $25 million which the minister is suggesting be offered for this purpose on credit terms.
To underline that I would also call attention to the fact that page 11 of the 1963 report made under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the amendment to which act was the subject of discussion yesterday, shows that $99 million-almost $100 million-in the year 1963 alone was utilized by the farmers in Canada for the purchase of farm machinery under the pertinent provisions of that legislation. In other words, the farmers of Canada purchased $100 million worth of farm equipment under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. It is interesting to note that there were

Farm Machinery
58,000 applications, and that the average loan per farmer was less than $2,000.
The next question I should like to ask the minister is this: To what particular portion of the farming community is this legislation dedicated? Who are contemplated as the beneficiaries under this legislation? The minister may, of course, say that under the Farm Improvement Loans Act it is impossible to grant loans to syndicates and co-operatives, and consequently they are the people who are shut out, under the provisions of that act, as a group, as a co-operative or as a syndicate, from securing these benefits. However, I would point out to the minister that under the Farm Credit Act, which he administers and which the previous government passed in 1959, section 2 defines "farming" as including a co-operative farm association and a family farming corporation. So it cannot be said at this time that prior to the enactment of the legislation which will be introduced following passage of this resolution there is not now in existence legislation which might well cover the particular groups the minister has in mind in this resolution.
It is rather interesting to note in examining the figures in connection with the Farm Credit Corporation-and I am now reading from the annual report and financial statement for the year 1963-64-that while for that year there were 8,689 loans totalling $108 million, with an average loan amount of $12,430, only 1.2 per cent of the loans were for the purchase of equipment. I would then assume-these are figures I do not have, but the minister may have them-that with regard to farm co-operatives and family farm incorporations, which are defined in the Farm Credit Act as being amongst the group who may secure the benefits of the legislation, a very infinitesimal portion of the total moneys lent would be lent to such groups for the purpose of securing farm machinery. Therefore I think this underlines the request I have made to the minister, that at some time he should enlighten members of the committee as to the groups, the people, the individuals who in his opinion are entitled and will be able to secure benefits from this particular legislation, having in mind the figures I have put on the record under the two enactments which at present constitute the sum total of federal farm credit legislation.
Before I sit down there is one more question I wish to ask the minister. This concerns a class of people who have not been mentioned in the debates we have had in the

house in connection with farm credit. I refer to the original settlers of this country, the Indians. I call the minister's attention to the fact that some years ago we had a joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons which inquired into the whole question of the Indian Act and the economic and social conditions of the Indian. One of the very interesting discussions which took place was with regard to the opportunities afforded to the Indian people under the Indian Act to secure the same types of benefits in the form of credit and assistance as did the other inhabitants of Canada.
It was then pointed out, not only by the Indians themselves but by officials of the department, that these people labour under a considerable handicap because of the fact they do not have title to their lands. Under the Indian Act they hold under what are known as certificates of occupation. As a resident of my province the minister will recall that there is an act known as the metis colonies act which sets up in the northern part of the province and to a large extent in my constituency a number of areas where those native inhabitants, who are no longer under the Indian Act but come under the metis act, secure certain benefits. Tracts of land have been set apart for their farms. They also operate under a system of land holding involving certificates of occupation which do not give them title to the land. Very often in their attempts to secure the benefits of the type of farm credit legislation and farm assistance programs available to other Canadians they come squarely up against this handicap. This was mentioned and extensively commented on and I would hope that in the legislation the minister is going to introduce provision will be made to deal with these people.
It is all very well to say, as has been said, that it is possible to change the provisions of the Indian Act so that Indians can hold title to their lands. At the present time the Indians themselves are very much opposed to this. When we are attempting to establish many of these people and to provide them with the opportunity to attain the living conditions that prevail for all other Canadians, I think it is manifestly unfair that because of their system of land ownership we should deprive them of the opportunities which they would receive under legislation of this kind. I know that many of these people are good farmers and would like the opportunity to settle into the mainstream of our economic life, but by reason of these facts they are

prevented from doing so. When the minister introduces the legislation I hope it will provide for them. If it does not I hope he will consider making appropriate amendments for that purpose.

Mr. Chairman, having had the honour of being a member of the agricultural committee for a number of years I have always been interested in the problem of the cost of farm machinery, and I believe that every member of the house should have the same interest because of the fact that the agricultural economy is still one of the basic and most important economic factors in this great country. I was disappointed yesterday afternoon that the minister gave such a brief resume of the proposed legislation. It seemed to be a rather insipid introduction for something as important as this and consequently I have a few questions to ask. I do not think that members on this side of the house have any apologies to make if we wish to make a few brief remarks, and I can assure you mine will be brief.
Because of the fact that so little explanation was given in introducing the legislation to provide for the extension of farm machinery syndicates I feel we should place our queries on the record. I ask the same question that many members have asked. Will the legislation actually help those farmers who need help? In discussing the problem of the cost of farm machinery with the well established farmer operating on a large scale, I find he feels that because of the legislation with respect to the agricultural economy placed on the statute books by the previous government he has been able to pull himself out of the economic doldrums. Nevertheless he is interested in this legislation also. However it is those smaller farmers who operate the great majority of the 400,000 farms spread across this vast land about whom I am concerned. I am concerned as to whether this measure will actually work in practice.
I can see that a father and a couple of sons, or three brothers could apply to the Farm Credit Corporation and receive a loan up to $75,000 to provide machinery to operate a family farm unit but, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Timiskaming, farmers are free enterprisers and individualists. They are very much concerned about running their own operations. Looking at the matter from the psychological aspect I wonder what would happen if three or four farmers formed a syndicate to buy a tractor costing $8,000 to
Farm Machinery
$11,000, or a $10,000 combine for harvesting, particularly during a fall season such as we are experiencing at the present time.
Who would decide who would use the particular machine when the sun did come out? After all, farmers are most interested in good weather because they are so dependant on the elements. Every farmer wants to get out and do 10, 12 or 14 hours of combining while the weather is right. I am concerned whether there is any practical value to this legislation. I hope the minister will put forward some way of solving this problem when he brings the bill before us.
With respect to the maximum loan of $75,000 which is available under this measure I would ask this question. Will the small farmer take the risk of using his land as collateral in order to borrow to this extent? I find that farmers are most reluctant to incur any large debt unless they can see a reasonable prospect of repaying the loan. There is always the consideration whether the farmer will want to pledge his chattels and land as collateral for a loan of this size.
As has been pointed out by other speakers, there is another factor that enters into the picture where you have a co-operative enterprise for the buying of machinery involving four or five farmers who purchase a machine. Who will be responsible for the repairing of the machinery? Will the machinery be maintained? Not long ago one of our members was talking to one of the Russian visitors to Canada who were interested in our farming operations. This Russian visitor looked at the tractor and asked the farmer how old it was. The farmer said it was 11 years old. The Russian visitor immediately raised his eyebrows and asked how he maintained such a lifespan for a tractor. The farmer said that the individual who purchased it took pride in keeping up his machinery; he greased it regularly and repaired it regularly so that the life of the tractor was extended. He asked the Russian what the situation was in Russia. The reply was that when they bought machinery to operate their communal farms the lifespan was perhaps a year and a half or two years. You can see the difference. If we set up these syndicates, will the machinery have the normal life expectancy it should have under the free enterprise system?
We find today that we have a number of farmers who, by agreement, will have one farmer buy a tractor or a big combine. In order to help him finance the cost of this machine he will do some custom work in the

Farm Machinery
neighbourhood to supplement the work that has already been done by farmers who have combines of their own. In order to take advantage of the sunshine and get his crop harvested, a farmer will seek the help of this neighbour and this, in turn, helps to liquidate the cost of the investment. By injecting this new feature of the farm machinery syndicate into the picture, are we going to interfere with this operation that is already established?
I believe the hon. member for Acadia has already referred to vertical integration. We had quite a bit of discussion about this in the agriculture committee several years ago. I should like to see the bill before I make too many comments on the subject, but this is something we have to guard against. We should not be providing large sums of money to commercial operators who are not really farmers in the ordinary sense of the word but who, because this money is available, want to get into the agriculture picture and make a fast buck, as it were. We want to be careful we are not encouraging further vertical integration.
The cost-price squeeze was referred to by some members. I believe the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam dwelt upon it at length. This is an old phrase, but I believe it has importance in the agricultural economy. I am wondering, in relation to the cost-price squeeze about which we speak, if we are putting the emphasis in the right place. We are interested in the high cost of machinery. I find in talking to the farmers in my area that a number of them are asking questions about the prices of the farm products they have to sell. We talk a lot about keeping down the prices of the things the farmer has to buy, but can we do something about raising the price of the things the farmer has to sell? I think this is an important aspect that has not been given too much consideration by the present government. We brought in several measures, of course, to help alleviate this condition. The Agricultural Stabilization Act is well known and well established now and has gone a long way toward helping the situation. I think it should be looked at again and perhaps made more effective in the light of the experience we have had since that legislation was introduced.
Another thing we did which helped to reduce this cost price squeeze was to get ourselves into a sellers' market so far as our wheat was concerned. As the members of the committee know, when we took office in 1957 and 1958 there was a large volume of grain

in the prairie provinces and there were high storage costs on it. By getting out and making contracts with other countries, we got ourselves into a liquid position. We got into a sellers' market, with the result that when the last world wheat agreement was completed some three years ago we got the world wheat price up 10 cents or 12 cents a bushel.
The next major move, and the most effective of all, was the revaluation of the Canadian dollar. This in effect placed another 15 cents per bushel on the value of our Canadian wheat. This 25 cents per bushel extra, when applied to a crop of 400 million bushels, which is a modest average production in western Canada, gave us another $100 million which did not come out of the pockets of the taxpayers, but came out of world markets. This was another step in reducing the cost-price squeeze.
I suggest to the committee that we have to look at both sides of this picture so far as the machine dealers are concerned. I understand that a number of machine dealers in various parts of the country have been able to grant a little higher value on the trade-ins. This has worked to the benefit of the purchaser. The machine dealers have been able to recover these increased costs by putting this machinery out for custom use in the neighbourhood. Again, some farmers in the neighbourhood who want to take advantage of the good weather will go in to the machine dealer and rent some of this farm machinery. They take it out to the farm, put it to work and then bring it back to the dealer. The result of this has been to help the dealer get his value out of the machine and to help the farmer get his crop harvested. It is a mutually satisfactory business and helps both sides. This practice has not been too widely developed as yet, but it has been developed and it would be a mistake to interfere with it.
The hon. member for Timiskaming said something about the former government not taking action so far as the agriculture committee was concerned in connection with this inquiry into the price of farm machinery. As a member of that committee I may say that it was one of the most worth-while committees of which I have ever been a member. We had 29 meetings and we heard witnesses from all across Canada, particularly those in the machine industry. We were not altogether satisfied with some of the testimony because we were repeatedly told that the answers to some questions would give information to competitors. Had we carried on as the government, we had arranged to have these wit-

nesses recalled. I was interested in hearing the hon. member for Jasper-Edson say that there were machine companies in Canada who were selling the same machines in Scotland for $600 less than in Canada. There was an indication of this sort of thing in the testimony given to the agriculture committee. As a result of that, we were prepared to recommend to the house that we send four or five men, one from each party in the house, on a short tour of Europe to look into the situation. However, the work of that committee was not completed. I do not believe we should bear too much criticism of the kind we received from the hon. member for Timiskaming, because I believe we would have been able to come up with very good results had we completed our work.
With these few remarks, I should like to suggest that before we finally pass this legislation it should be placed for some time at least in the hands of the committee on agriculture and colonization for further study.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Hays thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. C-121, to provide for the extension of credit to farm machinery syndicates.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

I had suggested that if it were at all possible for the present bill to be carried through its three stages, it would foe a different thing from the crop insurance bill, because the present bill, if it is passed, may 20220-513
