Crop Insurance Act CROP INSURANCE ACT

speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (Minister of Agriculture) moved
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That It is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Crop Insurance Act to authorize the governor in council to enter into agreements for the purpose of establishing a crop reinsurance program to supplement provincial crop insurance plans; to provide for the establishment in the consolidated revenue fund of a special account, to be known as the crop reinsurance fund, to which shall be credited amounts paid by a province under a crop reinsurance agreement and out of which shall be paid amounts required for the payment of reinsurance claims; to authorize advances from time to time from the consolidated revenue fund by way of non-interest bearing loans to the crop reinsurance fund; and to authorize the rebate, to grain growers whose grain is grown on insured lands, of sums paid by way of levy under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Batten in the chair.

Crop Insurance Act
1959, the minister of agriculture indicated that the lands operated by farmers who purchased crop insurance coverage under a provincial scheme would be excluded from benefits of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and that they would not be required to pay the 1 per cent P.F.A.A. levy on grain sales. However the act in its final form only provided that the initial payment farmers receive at the time of delivery of grain should be exempt from the levy. Interim and final payments made by the wheat board still remained subject to the levy. The reason for this was because of certain administrative problems encountered by the Canadian wheat board. We now feel we have a solution for these problems which will enable us to carry out the original intent of the act to exempt insured farmers from any payment of the levy.
As the house knows, only three provinces- Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Prince Edward Island-have so far joined in the program, although Alberta and Nova Scotia now have crop insurance legislation on their books. Manitoba has had the most ambitious crop insurance scheme so far. It is expected to cover some 6,200 farmers this year with about $15 million worth of insurance. Some 2,200 farmers have been insured in Saskatchewan and 75 in Prince Edward Island. Altogether that is about 8,500 of the 480,000 farms in all of Canada-not a very substantial proportion.
May I say in conclusion that the government believes this legislation will encourage more provinces to participate and encourage them to offer crop insurance coverage much more widely. This would mean crop insurance becoming available to many more farmers eventually, we hope, in every province thus removing their long-standing fear of being ruined overnight by disasters over which they or anyone else have no control.
By making the crop insurance program more effective with the changes this government proposes, there will be available a most important new stabilizing force, not just in our farm economy but, because of the importance of our farm economy to so many other areas of activity in this country, also in the economy of the country as a whole.

These amendments to the crop insurance legislation which was placed on the statute books by the previous government in 1959 are, I feel, a logical development in view of the experience of the government, and of the province of Manitoba

in particular in this field. When the legislation was introduced by the hon. member for Calgary North, he indicated that in the light of experience it might be necessary to introduce amendments from time to time so as to improve the act, bring it up to date and enable it to do the job it was intended to do in all circumstances.
I was interested in one comment the minister made. He said he was convinced of the value of crop insurance. We are pleased to know this, because the members of the party to which he belongs were by no means so convinced when they made their comments on the legislation brought forward in 1959. They said, as I recall, that it would be of little value or benefit to anybody and that farmers would not participate in the scheme. However the wisdom of the former government in introducing this legislation, as well as of the Manitoba government in following it up by complementary legislation, has clearly been justified. It has been shown that crop insurance is not only desirable but that it is almost a necessity in these days of high fixed costs and fluctuating yields.
This is not the only example of hon. members opposite being converted to programs initiated by the previous government. I recall the comments they had to make about sales of wheat to China. I remember how they beat around the country telling everyone that these sales were just a flash in the pan- the sort of thing that would not be repeated. I was interested in the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce some time ago when he said they are looking to China as a continuing market for wheat. I have digressed a little here, Mr. Chairman, but the minister gave us that opportunity a short while ago when he said he wanted to get this farm machinery syndicates bill through, and if we wanted to discuss farm problems generally we could discuss them on this bill. When we were discussing supplementary estimates I remember the minister suggested we should deal with general farm policy on the main estimates; and when we got to the main estimates he suggested we should deal with these matters on the particular items. Then when we reached that stage, the minister wanted us to discuss these questions somewhere else. I suppose that now we are dealing with the crop insurance resolution the minister will suggest that we discuss these matters on next year's estimates.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I would hope we can get this crop insurance legislation through for next spring, so it

is all right for the hon. member to speak as long as he wishes; but the farm machinery syndicates bill is wanted right away, so I hope we can get it through quickly.

I am not sure it is that urgent, Mr. Chairman; the crop is just about off the land and most of the farm machinery that will be required will not be required until next spring. However so far as this legislation is concerned, I think it is of great importance that it be dealt with at the earliest possible opportunity, because in my own province of Manitoba, which is the pioneer in the field of crop insurance, they have been asking for this legislation since 1962 and the government of that day-
Nineteen fifty eight.

My hon. friend is wrong, Mr. Chairman, because it was in 1962 that there was a formal presentation and request for a reinsurance proposition and there was an amendment to the existing act. We were dealing with it at the time, and I regret to say that there was some opposition to the introduction of this amendment to the crop insurance legislation. The opposition was from treasury board, because they felt it was going to cost the treasury too much money. However, this is certainly far from the truth, because rather than costing the treasury money, I feel this amendment to the legislation is going to save the treasury money.
The minister indicated that this legislation was going to afford the provinces an opportunity to expand their crop insurance program and enable them to get into the business of crop insurance under a more developed program than exists at the present time. I was speaking to the minister of agriculture of the province of Manitoba only yesterday, and he was very happy to learn that this legislation was coming forth, and was anxious that it should be passed as quickly as possible so they could extend their plans in regard to crop insurance to cover about 50 per cent of the farmers in that province for next year.
I sometimes feel that the public generally misunderstands the role of crop insurance in an over-all farm program. Crop insurance by itself is nothing more than a device that levels out yields from year to year. This is a very important function of a farm program. If we are to provide the degree of stability in agriculture that is necessary to maintain income levels that will take care of the high costs of production, this type of program is very necessary. In crop insurance we find one facet of a farm program that deals with the vari-
Crop Insurance Act
ability of income due to the fluctuation of yield. It is fairly obvious that crop insurance, taken by itself, can have no influence whatsoever on the variation of income due to price variations. Therefore another piece of legislation was introduced by the previous government to take care of that aspect of income variations. That policy was embodied in the provisions of the price stabilization bill, which does provide some degree of stability in prices, preventing the violent fluctuations of prices of agricultural products.
Then again there is a necessity to provide for credit to farmers, and this has been dealt with by the farm credit legislation, the Farm Improvement Loans Act and other items of legislation that deal with farm credit. Another program that was initiated by the previous government in an effort to provide greater stability on farms was a program of accelerated marketing research, a program that I feel is necessary if the increased production that is a result of better research, a better application of the products of research, is to find markets. These four items of the previous government's farm program-which, incidentally, were not too well received by the opposition at that time-have become the mainstay of the agricultural program and have formed the bulwark of the program designed to provide some stability in agricultural prices.
At the present time crop insurance in the province of Manitoba is extended to about 6,000 farmers, as the minister indicated, with a total liability of something like $14 million. At the time the program was initiated, in the 1960-61 crop year, something like 2,500 farmers signed up for the program, with a total liability of $4 million. With the provisions of this amendment to the Crop Insurance Act it is hoped that within the province of Manitoba the total liability next year, covering about 50 per cent of the farmers, will amount to something over $25 million.
We can readily see that with the extent of this coverage the liability assumed by the province is far greater than the resources that a provincial government is capable of bearing in the event of a disastrous crop loss. So the introduction of this legislation is designed to provide that the federal government will assume that liability; not at any loss, I might add, to the federal treasury over the long period, because the premiums being paid by the provinces will be actuarially sound and designed to take care of crop losses over a period of years.
The minister mentioned that the period of research that had gone into the development

Crop Insurance Act
of the crop insurance program went back 35 years. I think it was based largely on the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. I have always felt that for several reasons the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, although in some respects it might be followed, is not an accurate or reliable guide to follow in the developing and processing of data for crop insurance programs. First of all, in a crop insurance program there will be a number of areas that are engaged in the production of grain at the present time that will not be covered by crop insurance because the premiums, the risk factor, in those particular areas are too high for the farmers to take advantage of crop insurance. Therefore, in my opinion they will seek other forms of production, perhaps other forms of production more remunerative to those particular areas and perhaps more suitable for the type of soil in those regions. Second, Mr. Chairman, the advances that have been made in technology, in farming methods, over the past number of years would tend to minimize the risk factor as opposed to 35 years ago. I am speaking of the extensive use of pesticides, which have minimized crop losses due to insects, which was at one time a source of some difficulty which the farmers had to face in relation to crop yields. The use of insecticides and herbicides has done a great deal to increase production. Fertilizer application and more modem methods of farming have all contributed to higher average yields than was the case even in the 1930's. I think the figure for the average rainfall during the 1959-1964 period was far less than it was during the 1930's; yet the experience particularly of 1961, when the drought situation was considered quite severe in western Canada, shows that the yield for that year was much higher than any of the yields we experienced in the 1930's when the drought was perhaps not quite so severe. I think this can be attributed to the fact that farmers are taking advantage of the more modern methods of farming and are using more fertilizer, pesticides and herbicides. So I think that we can logically expect that the experience over the next few years of the incidence of crop loss will be that it will be lower than it was in the past number of years, and for that reason I think we can look forward with some degree of optimism to the application of crop insurance. Because of the risk factor the premiums will be lower and the cost to the farmer not as great as some people have anticipated.
I have heard many farmers, and indeed speakers in this house suggest that rather
[Mr. Jorgenson.l
than introducing amendments to crop insurance legislation, or even introducing crop insurance legislation itself, we should simply amend the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and develop that program to replace crop insurance. I should like to draw the attention of the committee to some of the difficulties which might be involved in amending the Prairie Farm Assistance Act to meet today's conditions, and if the variability of income due to crop losses is also to be met.
In 1939 P.F.A.A. was intended as a relief measure, and as such has done I think a creditable job over the years. The difficulty with the Prairie Farm Assistance Act regulations is that the regulations do not apply on an individual basis, and in my opinion it would be a mistake to attempt to make payments on an individual basis under P.F.A.A. unless some effort were made to amend the regulations so as to change the method of payment into the fund. At the present time the levy is imposed on the deliveries of grain to the elevator on the basis of 1 per cent of the value of the grain sold. If the levy were simply increased this would mean that those farmers selling the most grain-who ostensibly would be the farmers who were the most productive and successful-would be paying into the fund a great deal more than those farmers who suffered crop losses year after year. To a large extent it is obvious if one examines the record of P.F.A.A. that the majority of payments made under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act are in specific areas. If one examines these areas a little more carefully he will discover that to a large extent these areas are classed either as marginal or submarginal areas.
Therefore the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, although as I have said a creditable piece of legislation which has done a tremendous job over the years, is diametrically opposed to the attempt today to encourage the proper utilization of the land. We have two acts; we have the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act which is calculated and designed to encourage proper utilization of land, and more recently the ARDA legislation, which is intended to do the same thing. My view and my experience of prairie farm assistance is that it has the opposite effect and a tendency to encourage improper use of land, for the reason that there are two programs here diametrically opposed one to the other. The natural result is, first, confusion in the minds of the farmers, and second, an improper utilization of their resources.

I suggest to the committee that simply making amendments to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, of which there have been many, will not resolve this basic difficulty and take care of the situation I mentioned earlier with regard to the need for larger payments in the event of crop losses. Anyone with experience in farming today knows full well that a payment of $800, which is the maximum payment under P.F.A.A., will do nothing to offset the cost incurred by a farmer whose expenses amount perhaps to $10,000 to $15,000 a year. Something more realistic, something which will take care of the cost involved in production today, is necessary, and I feel that this legislation is the answer. I am glad to see that the minister has chosen this time to introduce this amendment, because in my opinion it is necessary if the provinces are to take advantage of the provisions of the Crop Insurance Act.
I might mention that under P.F.A.A. something like $330 million has been paid out up to the report of last year. At the same time there has been collected and paid in by the farmers themselves, I might add, some $142 million, with the difference of something like $187 million being taken up by the federal treasury. I would venture to suggest that the statistics developed by the crop insurance corporation in the province of Manitoba, as well as by the Department of Agriculture, clearly indicate that if crop insurance had been in effect during that same period of years in Manitoba the amount of money paid into the province under crop insurance would have been considerably less than the amount paid under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, and the benefits to the farmer would have been considerably greater.
Every argument I have attempted to put forward here this afternoon on behalf of crop insurance indicates that the need for this legislation and amendment to this legislation is very great, and we are certainly pleased that the minister has finally introduced this amendment. But in saying that, we hope the government do not take the stand that this particular amendment to the crop insurance legislation is going to be the final word on crop insurance, because it is far from that. Crop insurance, like any other program, must be continuing. It must be continuously examined in the light of existing conditions and amended wherever necessary. As I said earlier, there need be no fear on the part of the government that because it has introduced this legislation there is going
Crop Insurance Act
to be a great deal more expense incurred by the federal treasury. In my view there will be far less because there are many ad hoc programs now in effect to take care of crop disasters. We had an example of this recently in the Ottawa valley, when the provisions of the feed grain assistance program were implemented to provide assistance to farmers who suffered losses of hay and losses from starving cattle, a fact which was dramatically portrayed in a picture I saw in one of the Ottawa newspapers. I recall that a number of years ago the crops in western Canada were unharvested and remained out all winter and some assistance was provided at that time. Disaster loans have been provided. All of these ad hoc arrangements, which are designed to take care of particular situations arising from time to time, can fully and completely be taken care of under a comprehensive crop insurance program. For this reason, as I said earlier there need be no fear on the part of the government or on the part of anyone in the country that vast sums of money from the federal treasury will be poured into this program, because such is not the case.
The first two provisions of the measure stipulate that the federal government shall pay 20 per cent of the premiums and 50 per cent of the administration costs of the money paid out. This is true, but it is no more than is being done under the provisions of the unemployment insurance fund. In my opinion this is not so costly that the people of Canada cannot assume this responsibility, when you consider the value received for the dollars they put in, when you consider the stability it provides for agriculture and when you consider that agricultural stability provides stability in the economy because farmers are able to purchase the machinery and other things they require, which keeps the factories and the people working in those factories busy.
This was amply demonstrated within the past year. The huge sales of wheat to communist China and Russia and the buoyant market situation have provided a buoyant economy in this country, and I think to a large extent this is a reflection of the ability of the farmers to purchase these items of machinery. Anything that can be done to provide for real stability in agriculture is money well spent, as far as I am concerned.
Again, I do not think it is necessary for us to limit our sights to the provision of crop insurance for crops only. What is wrong with thinking in terms of catch insurance

Crop Insurance Act
for fishermen? What is wrong with thinking in terms of providing insurance for hay crops as well as potato, other vegetable and tobacco crops? All these crops can be profitably insured and provide the degree of stability which, as I said earlier, is so necessary today to meet the high costs of production.
In my own province of Manitoba the crop insurance corporation has provided for the efficient farmer, the farmer who is farming his land in the best possible manner, the opportunity to get his insurance somewhat cheaper. This is based on the same principle as ordinary insurance. Where the risk factor is smaller the premiums are smaller. The result is better farming methods, which the government simply must encourage, and a lower cost to the farmer for insuring his crop. In addition, it is consistent with our aim of maximizing the efficient use of all our resources, human, financial and land.
In conclusion I should like to read the last paragraph of a statement made by the minister of agriculture of the province of Manitoba, Hon. George Hutton, to the federal-provincial conference on agriculture held in Ottawa in 1962. I think this is something that will give us some food for thought when we are considering this legislation.
He said:
We think that there is one question that should be squarely faced-should governments sit back and be forced by circumstances into programs which may be mediocre or poorly planned or do governments have some responsibility to sell a program of value to the farm community?
This is certainly my opinion so far as crop insurance is concerned. I am somewhat distressed by the reluctance of some provincial governments to participate more fully in a crop insurance program.
For generations the threat of crop loss due to natural disaster has hung like a cloud over the farmer of Canada, especially in the west. We know that the loss of production has been the most significant factor in years of low income to farmers and the largest contributing factor to instability in farm income. I think that if you will study the principles of crop insurance you will find an application to your province. You will find that there is a planned approach to this whole question of assistance at times of crop disaster. The farmers are ready; the farmers are willing. We should be too.
I think this sums up my attitude with respect to this legislation, and again I should like to thank the minister for introducing it at this time.

Mr. Chairman, the members of this party have always been strong supporters of the idea of crop insurance. As far

back as 30 years ago we placed in our program crop insurance and unemployment insurance as two of the methods of protecting people against a disastrous decline in income. We advocated at that time that there should be unemployment insurance for those who, through no fault of their own, were thrown out of work and that at the same time there ought to be crop insurance for those farmers who, also through no fault of their own, were deprived of their normal livelihood. We campaigned very hard for that during the 1930's and for that reason we welcomed the Prairie Farm Assistance Act when it was introduced in 1939, and we supported that measure.
I have always looked upon the P.F.A.A. as really being the farmers' equivalent of unemployment insurance. While it is true, as the previous speaker said, that the government of Canada has had to subsidize P.F.A.A., it is equally true of course that the unemployment insurance fund is subsidized, since its revenue is made up of a three way split, contributions by the employee, employer and the government of Canada. Therefore I do not think that prairie farmers need to apologize at any time for the fact that the 1 per cent levy on their grain which they contribute to the fund has not been sufficient to cover the cost, with the result that over the period of years since 1939 very considerable contributions from the federal treasury have been required.
I am one of those who felt that the P.F.A.A. legislation could be revamped and extended into a genuine national crop insurance plan. I agree completely with the last speaker that it would have to be almost entirely revamped and reorganized in order to make the P.F.A.A. system applicable across Canada and applicable to all the different types of farmers on an equitable basis. I think this could have been done, however. To do this it would have been necessary to divide the country into regions and each province into regions. I think the levy would have to vary from district to district according to the productivity of that area so that the levy would be higher in high risk areas and lower in the good crop communities.
I also think, as he does, that to have extended P.F.A.A. and make it a national crop insurance plan it would have been necessary to insure farmers on an individual basis. But that is not as difficult now as it would have been 25 years ago because the farmer has his permit book from the Canadian wheat board, he has to register how many acres he

is sowing to different kinds of crops and the government has a record of every bushel he delivers to the elevator. Therefore it would not be as difficult now as it would have been 25 years ago to pay benefits from a national crop insurance plan on an individual basis.
The problem of the farmer who stays on land which should be taken out of production would be met to a very large extent by varying the levy according to the area and according to the production record. It would also have been necessary to extend the benefits of a national crop insurance plan organized on the P.F.A.A. pattern to cover crops other than cereal grains. I think this might have been done. I was very sorry at the time it was not done because I think P.F.A.A. had caught the imagination of the farmers. It had demonstrated its worth as a stabilizing factor in farm income.
I still think, had it been extended into a national crop insurance plan the farmers would have accepted it. It would still have been possible to take advantage of that and to have had crop insurance either run by private insurance companies or by municipal hail insurance groups, or by provincial governments to provide additional crop insurance if the farmers wanted it. I think a national crop insurance plan that would have provided a minimum guaranteed return to every farmer in the event of a crop failure would have been accepted and would have been extremely beneficial. I have always regretted that this step was not taken.
Instead, in 1959 the Crop Insurance Act which it is now proposed to amend was brought into effect. I think all members will agree that it has not been an outstanding success in terms of the extent to which farmers have availed themselves of it. Only three provinces have entered into agreements with the federal government. In the case of Prince Edward Island only 75 farmers, I think, come under the plan, so one can virtually rule them out and say that really there are only two provinces, Manitoba and Saskatchewan, that have made any extensive use of this plan. Now, a national crop insurance plan that covers in all of Canada only about 6,000 farmers out of 400,000 farmers is a long way from a national crop insurance program.
There is no doubt in my mind as to why there has not been greater acceptance of this plan. The crop insurance plan that was introduced in 1959 transferred from the federal government to the provincial governments what had been solely a federal responsibility. It laid upon provincial governments a respon-20220-514
Crop Insurance Act
sibility which they could not possibly discharge if that plan went beyond a merely pilot project stage. Up until 1959, the entire cost of operating crop insurance that we had under P.F.A.A. was met either from the 1 per cent levy which a farmer paid on his deliveries of grain, or from the federal treasury. But when crop insurance was introduced the provincial governments, that had up until that time no financial responsibility whatever, found that they were to be called upon to pay, first of all, 50 per cent of the administrative costs; second; since the federal government was paying 20 per cent of the premium costs the provinces were expected to match this, so the provinces were now called upon to pay 20 per cent of the premium costs. These two items, if the plan were to have very widespread acceptance, could amount to a considerable sum of money.
However, I do not believe that was the main reason the provinces were cautious and reluctant about entering into crop insurance. What really frightened the provinces was the fact that under the crop insurance legislation they were underwriting the entire cost of a large scale crop failure. Under the act as it now stands, in the event of a crop failure if the reimbursements exceed the amount of the premiums which have been collected and the reserves which have been built up, the provinces must pay the first $200,000. They may then borrow from the federal government 75 per cent of the balance. What does this mean? It means that in addition to the provinces paying 50 per cent of the administrative costs and 20 per cent of the premiums they could, in the case of a severe crop failure, be called upon to pay $200,000 plus 25 per cent of the balance of the cost of the crop failure, and accept as a contingent liability the other 75 per cent.
As long as the crop insurance plan is on such a very small scale as it has been in Manitoba and Saskatchewan, this has not been a serious problem. However, every member here knows that if we had any of the catastrophic crop failures such as we have had in some parts of Canada, particularly the prairies, if we had a drought, frost or an infestation of grasshoppers or a severe rust epidemic which took out an entire crop-and this has happened in the past-the amount for which the provincial government could find itself responsible might be in the tens of millions or even hundreds of millions of dollars, if the plan covered every farmer in the province. This is why the provinces have been extremely wary about rushing

Crop Insurance Act
into a crop insurance agreement with, the federal government or to sign up farmers on a very large scale. I must say, Mr. Chairman, that I do not believe we will ever have a national crop insurance plan unless the federal government is prepared to accept a much larger share of the financial responsibility than they are doing under the present legislation.
It is true that in the legislation which the minister is now bringing down this burden is ameliorated somewhat. There is to be some provision for reinsurance and some additional assistance by the federal government if the provinces get into financial difficulty. I do not want to discuss the details of that until we have had a chance to look at the bill itself. The point I want to make is that even the provisions which are outlined now by the minister are not sufficiently generous to make it possible for the provinces, with any degree of enthusiasm, to enter into a crop insurance arrangement. Unless the federal government is prepared to assume by far the major portion of the financial responsibility and leave to the provinces mainly the administration and a very small financial contribution, we are not going to have crop insurance on a nation-wide basis.
This crop insurance plan we have at the moment is simply a pilot project. It will be useful in the future to farmers who have availed themselves of it. It will be useful to the government in that it will enable them to gather statistics, to work out techniques, by which crop insurance may be improved and extended. If the minister wants to do something for the farmers he had better start working on a national crop insurance plan, and if he wants such a plan to be accepted, then he must either make it a national plan, operated by the government of Canada, similar to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, or if he wants to decentralize he must be prepared to offer the provinces much more generous terms than those contained in the present act, or those forecast in the legislation he proposes to bring down.

In the few minutes left before we rise I would like to say that the resolution before us is a step in the right direction toward a national, comprehensive crop insurance scheme, but in my view it is a very limited step.
I must draw your attention, Mr. Chairman, to the fact that there seems to be a great
degree of unanimity between the Conservative party, the New Democratic party and the Social Credit party with respect to some of the lessons we have learned over the years regarding crop insurance, and particularly the provisions of P.F.A.A. As has been pointed out a number of times today, this legislation requires complementary legislation to be passed by the provincial legislatures before it has effect in any of the provinces.
It has been pointed out that for a number of years there have been pilot projects in Manitoba and Saskatchewan and that these projects have not been completely satisfactory. We also know that Prince Edward Island has very timidly moved into this field, and that during the past session the Alberta provincial legislature considered legislation to set up a crop insurance program. Up to the present time these programs have not been too successful, but on the other hand we have had 25 years experience evolving a satisfactory crop insurance scheme within P.F.A.A. for most of the prairies. It would be unfortunate if we were to try to sidestep all of the experience and practice that has come from that operation.
Progress reported.
